tensor.label: Tensor workloads
tensor.rubric: Tensor workloads (qualitative): how naturally a tool expresses dense array maths (batched linear algebra, convolutions, broadcasting) and how much of it its tuned libraries cover. 5 = this is its home ground.
tensor.anchor: 5 = dense array maths, batched linear algebra and convolutions are its home ground.

PyTorch.reason: Dense array maths is its home ground, with tuned libraries behind batched linear algebra, convolutions and broadcasting.

JAX.reason: Array programs written once and compiled by XLA; batched linear algebra, convolutions and broadcasting are first-class.

CuPy.reason: A NumPy-shaped API over the CUDA math libraries; it covers most dense array work.

NumPy.reason: The reference API for dense array maths and broadcasting on the CPU, with tuned BLAS and LAPACK underneath.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: Per-thread kernels are its home ground; it also offers matrix and tile types for dense blocks.

raptor.reason: Batched small dense algebra per lane; large products, solvers and tuned libraries go to PyTorch/JAX zero-copy.

Numba.reason: Compiles loops and NumPy-style code; np.linalg is supported on the CPU through the BLAS and LAPACK it calls.

array_style.label: Array-style programming
array_style.rubric: Array-style programming (qualitative): how naturally you write whole-array expressions eagerly, the NumPy way. 5 = the array expression is the programming model. Scores are the author's judgement.
array_style.anchor: 5 = the whole-array expression is the programming model.

NumPy.reason: The whole-array expression is the programming model, evaluated eagerly; the right choice for array code on the CPU.

CuPy.reason: The NumPy way on the GPU: whole-array expressions, run eagerly.

PyTorch.reason: Eager tensor expressions are the programming model.

JAX.reason: NumPy-style array expressions, but functional and traced rather than eager.

Numba.reason: You mostly write loops over arrays; array expressions are secondary.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: You write per-thread kernels; whole-array expressions are not the model.

raptor.reason: A per-sample kernel language by design: you write one step of one sample, and whole-array code is left to array libraries, with which raptor exchanges arrays zero-copy.

half_precision.label: Half precision and below
half_precision.rubric: Half precision and below (qualitative): FP16, BF16, FP8 and FP4 arithmetic and tensor cores (FP32 and FP64 are measured on the other axes). 5 = these formats and tensor cores are first-class paths. Scores are the author's judgement.
half_precision.anchor: 5 = FP16, BF16, FP8, FP4 and tensor cores are first-class paths.

PyTorch.reason: FP16, BF16 and FP8 types with tensor-core paths, including autocast.

JAX.reason: FP16, BF16 and FP8 types, with XLA targeting tensor cores.

CuPy.reason: float16 arrays and half-precision BLAS calls; tensor-core use comes through the libraries.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: float16 support and tile operations that can use tensor cores.

NumPy.reason: float16 storage and arithmetic are a supported path, though slow on the CPU and nothing below it.

Numba.reason: float16 arithmetic intrinsics in numba.cuda are a supported path; no BF16/FP8 or tensor-core path.

raptor.reason: Not supported. raptor is scoped to FP32 and FP64 numerics; half-precision and tensor-core work belongs with PyTorch or JAX.

control.label: Low-level control
control.rubric: Low-level control (qualitative): how much of the GPU's execution you control from the tool's own language: thread indexing, shared memory, atomics, launch shape, synchronisation (raw CUDA/C++ not counted). 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched. On a CPU the same question is asked of threads, SIMD and memory layout. Scores are the author's judgement.
control.anchor: 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: You write the per-thread kernel and choose its launch: near-total control short of raw CUDA, the right choice for hand-tuned kernels.

Numba.reason: numba.cuda gives thread indexing, shared memory, atomics and explicit launch shapes, the right choice when you want to manage the GPU by hand.

JAX.reason: Pallas exposes kernel-level control; plain JAX leaves scheduling to XLA.

CuPy.reason: Element-wise and reduction kernels; full control only through raw CUDA.

PyTorch.reason: Operators and a few custom-kernel hooks; launches are left to the framework.

raptor.reason: Per-sample indexing (sample_index, split_index), reads of any sample (.at) and sums and scatters across samples (hawk.sum, hawk.scatter); launch shape, shared memory and kernel-level synchronisation stay with hawk and eagle, while graph-level ordering (forks, waits, device-side branches and loops) is yours, so compaction can adapt to uneven batches. For hand-tuned thread-level kernels, Warp or Numba is the right choice.

JAX.reason: Plain JAX leaves threads, vectorisation and layout to XLA; Pallas control is aimed at the GPU.

NumPy.reason: Strides and memory layout are yours to choose; threads and SIMD are left to the libraries underneath.

Numba.reason: prange, explicit threads and typed loops; SIMD and memory layout are yours.

single_thread.label: Single-thread abstraction
single_thread.rubric: Single-thread abstraction (qualitative): how fully you can write the code for one sample, one step, and let the tool run it over the batch: threads, launches, early stopping and scheduling included. 5 = you write one sample and nothing else. Scores are the author's judgement.
single_thread.anchor: 5 = you write one sample and nothing else.

raptor.reason: You write one step of one sample, on a grid of several axes if the problem has them; hawk and eagle handle threads, launches, stopping and compaction, including compaction in groups.

JAX.reason: A per-sample function under vmap; early stopping becomes masking you write.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: A per-thread kernel: you index and loop yourself, and choose the launch.

PyTorch.reason: torch.func.vmap over a per-sample function; stopping and batching stay with you.

Numba.reason: A per-index body under prange or cuda.jit; indexing and launch are yours.

CuPy.reason: Element-wise kernels run per element; the batching logic is yours.

NumPy.reason: Whole-array code; there is no per-sample model.

differentiable.label: Differentiable kernels
differentiable.rubric: Differentiable kernels (qualitative): how directly you get forward- and reverse-mode derivatives of your own kernels, on GPU and on CPU. 5 = built in for every kernel written in the tool's own vocabulary.
differentiable.anchor: 5 = derivatives are built in for every kernel written in the tool.

PyTorch.reason: Autograd differentiates tensor programs; a custom kernel needs its backward written by hand.

JAX.reason: Forward and reverse mode through grad, jvp and vjp, on GPU and CPU.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: Reverse mode through wp.Tape over its kernels, with its emphasis on reverse mode over the tape.

CuPy.reason: No automatic differentiation; it is usually paired with a framework that has one.

raptor.reason: Every kernel written in hawk's own vocabulary carries generated forward- and reverse-mode derivatives on GPU and CPU, including through parameter-dependent branches (jump=), events and, with the rolled reverse pass, a Dispatch inside a loop and a graph builder's device branches and loops (skippable, repeat_while); second order is written jvp(vjp).

NumPy.reason: No automatic differentiation of its own.

Numba.reason: No automatic differentiation of its own.

arrays.label: Works with your arrays
arrays.rubric: Works with your arrays (qualitative): how freely arrays move to and from other frameworks without copies. 5 = zero-copy exchange is the norm.
arrays.anchor: 5 = zero-copy exchange with other frameworks is the norm.

PyTorch.reason: DLPack and the array interface exchange tensors with other libraries, mostly without copies.

JAX.reason: DLPack exchange with other frameworks, mostly without copies.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: Zero-copy views of PyTorch, JAX and NumPy arrays.

CuPy.reason: Its arrays are the common currency of the CUDA array world, with DLPack and the CUDA array interface.

raptor.reason: Zero-copy through DLPack with a certified matrix (CuPy, PyTorch, Warp, JAX and NumPy).

NumPy.reason: The array protocols everyone reads, on the host; device memory is out of its scope.

Numba.reason: Reads NumPy arrays directly and exposes the CUDA array interface; wider exchange takes some glue.

deploy.label: Deploy outside Python
deploy.rubric: Deploy outside Python (qualitative): whether a compiled kernel can run from programs that are not Python. 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.
deploy.anchor: 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.

PyTorch.reason: TorchScript, AOT export and a C++ runtime take models into non-Python programs.

JAX.reason: Compiled XLA programs can be exported and run from other runtimes.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: Captured graphs and compiled modules replay from a standalone C++ program on CUDA and on the CPU device; the Warp runtime is still needed.

CuPy.reason: Lives in Python; its kernels are not packaged for other programs.

raptor.reason: A compiled kernel runs from any program that can load its manifest (eagle is the loader today), and hawk's c target writes standalone MISRA C with no Python and no eagle.

NumPy.reason: A Python library; nothing is compiled into a separate artefact.

Numba.reason: Ahead-of-time compilation exists in a limited form; most use stays inside Python.

extensible.label: Extensibility
extensible.rubric: Extensibility (qualitative): how readily new hardware, backends and features can be added without losing speed. 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets. Scores are the author's judgement.
extensible.anchor: 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets.

JAX.reason: XLA and PJRT plugins add new hardware backends.

PyTorch.reason: Out-of-tree backends and custom operators are supported.

raptor.reason: A plugin registry and a protocol spine; two execution backends today (CUDA and CPU threads) and a third hawk target, standalone C; no second vendor yet. Adding a target (a row in hawk's target table) or an execution backend (a C seam of seven required functions) is a documented path, so the extension work is written down.

Numba.reason: An extension API for new types and targets, at a low level.

NumPy.reason: Array-API dispatch lets other array libraries stand in.

NVIDIA Warp.reason: NVIDIA GPUs and the CPU; no public path to add a backend.

CuPy.reason: Runs on CUDA and ROCm GPUs; the score is the author's judgement of its extension path.
